desc:
You must delete exactly one character from the string s (choose any position). Different positions can lead to the same resulting string.

Return the number of distinct strings that can be obtained this way. The empty string counts as a string when s has length 1.

s = "aabbc"  ->  3   ("abbc", "aabc", "aabb")
s = "abc"    ->  3
s = "aaaa"   ->  1
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Deleting every position and storing the results in a set works for short strings, but each result costs O(n) to build.
When do two different deletions give the same string? Look at deleting positions i < j and compare what is left.
They give the same string exactly when all characters from i to j are equal, so each block of equal adjacent letters contributes one result. Count the blocks.
editorial: Delete position i versus position j > i. The two results agree outside the range [i, j]. Inside it, the first result keeps s[i+1..j] and the second keeps s[i..j-1]. These are equal precisely when s[i] = s[i+1] = ... = s[j]. So deleting any character of a maximal block of equal letters yields the same string, and deleting from different blocks yields different strings.
The answer is therefore the number of maximal runs of equal letters: one plus the number of positions where s[i] != s[i-1]. This is a single O(n) scan with O(1) extra space.
